title: How many classrooms fit in one square kilometre?
description: A square kilometre is a square with each side one thousand metres, so it holds one million square metres. A classroom of eight metres by six metres covers forty eight square metres, and the one million is shared into classrooms of that size. Keeko takes a square kilometre as one thousand square metres.
teaching_notes: One idea: a square kilometre is a thousand metres by a thousand metres, so it holds a million square metres. Watch for students who take a square kilometre as one thousand square metres.

source: Larger areas are measured in square kilometres; how many square metres make a square kilometre, and how many classrooms of 8 m by 6 m fit in one
video_script.why: The child knows the area of a rectangle and that a kilometre is a thousand metres, and here meets square kilometres, as the book does.
video_script.substitution: The classroom of eight metres by six metres is a size chosen here; the book leaves the classroom to the child.
video_script.anchor: a classroom floor, eight metres by six metres, set against a square kilometre of land
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says one square kilometre is one thousand square metres, because a kilometre is a thousand metres. That area is only a thin strip one metre wide along one side of the square.
video_script.payoff_line: About twenty thousand eight hundred thirty three classrooms fit in one square kilometre.

final_answer.spoken: about twenty thousand eight hundred thirty three classrooms

maths_rules: check by rounding 48 up to 50: 1000000 / 50 = 20000; 48 is less than 50, so the number is a bit more than 20000
Keeko: 1000 m2 is a strip 1 m wide and 1000 m long; the square holds 1000 such strips
video_script.design: A small classroom floor stays beside a big square marked one kilometre on each side. The classroom is copied into the big square only in the working, and Keeko's thin strip is drawn along one side of the big square.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about large areas.
<bookmark mark='room'/>A classroom floor is eight metres by six metres.
<bookmark mark='land'/>A big square of land is one kilometre on each side.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many such classrooms would fit on that land?

beats.on_screen: the classroom and the big square stay on the board and Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the big square with each side marked 1 km = 1000 m; its area is called a square kilometre

marks.side: each side of the big square is marked 1 km = 1000 m
marks.name: the words square kilometre are written inside it

narration: <bookmark mark='side'/>One kilometre is one thousand metres.
<bookmark mark='name'/>A square with each side one kilometre is called a square kilometre.

beats.on_screen: Given: classroom 8 m by 6 m; land 1 km by 1 km

marks.given: the classroom sides and the land sides are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a classroom is eight metres by six metres, and the land is one kilometre by one kilometre.

beats.on_screen: To find: how many classrooms fit in 1 km²

marks.find: the words how many classrooms fit in 1 km² are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how many classrooms fit in one square kilometre.

marks.rule: the rule length × breadth is written
marks.val: 8 × 6 = 48 m² is written inside the classroom

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step one, find the classroom. Its area is length times breadth, eight times six.
<bookmark mark='val'/>That gives forty eight square metres.

marks.sides: 1000 m is written along both sides of the big square

narration: <bookmark mark='sides'/>Step two, change the land to square metres. Both sides are one thousand metres.
<bookmark mark='area'/>The area is one thousand times one thousand, which is one million square metres.

marks.share: 1,000,000 m² is shared into rooms of 48 m² each

narration: <bookmark mark='share'/>Step three, share the land into classrooms, forty eight square metres each.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>One million divided by forty eight.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check by rounding 48 up to 50: 1,000,000 ÷ 50 = 20,000, and 48 is less than 50, so the number is a bit more than 20,000
narration: <bookmark mark='round'/>Step four, check by rounding forty eight up to fifty.
<bookmark mark='est'/>One million divided by fifty is twenty thousand. Forty eight is a little less than fifty. The answer should be a bit more than twenty thousand.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>About twenty thousand eight hundred thirty three classrooms fit in one square kilometre.
<bookmark mark='near'/>That is a bit more than twenty thousand, as the check said.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the big square
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

marks.strip: a strip 1 m wide and 1000 m long is shaded along one edge of the big square
marks.rest: the rest of the big square is shaded in the warning colour
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and 1000 × 1000 is written

beats.colours: warning colour for the part of the big square left empty
narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks one square kilometre is one thousand square metres, because a kilometre is a thousand metres.
<bookmark mark='strip'/>But that area fills only a thin strip, one metre wide, along one edge.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>Nearly all of the big square is still empty.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>One thousand such strips fill the square. We multiply one thousand by one thousand.
